Conductivity Calculation

In this tutorial, we will show how to compute the phonon-limited electrical conductivity of nonmagnetic metal Al, ferromagnetic metal Fe, and intrinsic electron mobility of polar semiconductor GaAs using the self-energy relaxation time approximation (ERTA) and the linearised iterative Boltzmann transport equation (IBTE) via QTrans using cal_mode: 'conductivity'. The relevant theories are briefly introduced in the Conductivity section.

Warning

The following tutorials are designed for instructional purposes. To save computation time, the parameter settings are simplified and the results are not fully converged.

Bulk fcc Al

The bulk fcc aluminum tutorial is located in tutorials/Al/openmx/conductivity/. All necessary data files are available in tutorials/Al/openmx/data/. Reference outputs are provided in tutorials/Al/openmx/conductivity/ref/ , which can be used to compare with your own results to verify that QTrans is running correctly.

Once QTrans is installed in your Conda environment, you can easily run the following tutorials.

The calculation directory contains input-dense.yaml, input-sparse.yaml, and the reference outputs in ref/. The dense input reads grad_mat.npy, while the sparse input reads grad_mat_sparse.npy and enables advanced.read_sparse_grad_mat. Compare their results to check the effect of sparsification for this system.

cd tutorials/Al/openmx/conductivity/ && ls
input-dense.yaml  input-sparse.yaml ref/

Activate the Conda environment in which QTrans is installed:

conda activate QTrans

1. Self-energy relaxation time approximation (ERTA)

Here, we perform a QTrans calculation to calculate the conductivity of fcc aluminum on the 32x32x32 k-point and q-point grids using the self-energy relaxation time approximation (ERTA) with the dense gradient matrix.

You can first check the input flags in input-dense.yaml and make sure you understand the meaning of each tag. We consider the first six bands by setting bands_indices: '1-6', and choose an energy window with a half-width of 0.2 eV, using over_band_edge: 0.2. This window is highlighted as the yellow region in Figure 1. The temperature is set to the room temperature with temperature: 300.0. The method used here is ERTA, which is also the default method: mob_level: erta.

The complete input-dense.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3, 0, 0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Al-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [32,32,32]
  q_size: [32,32,32]
  bands_indices: '1-6'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 40
  smearq: 40
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 120

conductivity:
  mob_level: erta
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250

You can launch the QTrans calculation with:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-dense.yaml > dense_kq32_erta.out

At the end of the run, you should see output like this:

Conductivity(Siemens/m)           x                y                z
       x                2.7448e+07      -5.3200e-10       2.8235e-11
       y               -1.5477e-11       2.7448e+07      -4.4361e-11
       z               -4.0703e-11       1.6774e-11       2.7448e+07

This result is consistent with the symmetry of the FCC structure, where only the diagonal components of the conductivity tensor are non-zero.

The complete input-sparse.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Al-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [32,32,32]
  q_size: [32,32,32]
  bands_indices: '1-6'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 40
  smearq: 40
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 120

conductivity:
  mob_level: erta
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250

You can also use input-sparse.yaml with read_sparse_grad_mat setting to True in the advanced block to use the sparse gradient matrix and then compare the accuracy and runtime with the dense gradient matrix case:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-sparse.yaml > sparse_kq32_erta.out

Conductivity(Siemens/m)           x                y                z
       x                2.7459e+07      -2.2723e-10       1.7939e-12
       y               -1.1716e-10       2.7459e+07      -9.3805e-12
       z               -2.3320e-11       1.0818e-11       2.7459e+07

The diagonal components agree within approximately 0.04% for this example. Runtime depends on the gradient sparsity, hardware, and parallel configuration.

2. Iterative Boltzmann transport equation (IBTE)

You can also compute the conductivity of aluminum using the iterative Boltzmann transport equation (IBTE). IBTE uses the same input variables as ERTA, except for setting mob_level: ibte. Set ibte_error for the convergence threshold and ibte_cycle for the maximum number of iterations.

Both supplied OpenMX Al inputs select ERTA. Copy each input and set conductivity.mob_level: ibte before running IBTE. For example, save the following complete configuration as input-dense-ibte.yaml:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3, 0, 0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Al-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [32,32,32]
  q_size: [32,32,32]
  bands_indices: '1-6'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 40
  smearq: 40
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 120

conductivity:
  mob_level: ibte
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250

Run QTrans with:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-dense-ibte.yaml > dense_kq32_ibte.out

You should find output like this:

====================================================================================================
Iteration number:   19
====================================================================================================
Conductivity(Siemens/m)           x                y                z
       x                3.4041e+07      -7.5180e-10      -5.8462e-11
       y               -2.9355e-10       3.4041e+07       1.6475e-11
       z               -6.0094e-12       4.4908e-11       3.4041e+07

Converged in 19 cycles with error = 5.2005e-06

IBTE converged in 19 iterations, with a maximum error of \(5.2005\times 10^{-6}\) Siemens/m for conductivity tensors. IBTE also reports the initial ERTA solution before iteration.

For the sparse IBTE run, save the following as input-sparse-ibte.yaml:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Al-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [32,32,32]
  q_size: [32,32,32]
  bands_indices: '1-6'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 40
  smearq: 40
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 120

conductivity:
  mob_level: ibte
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config input-sparse-ibte.yaml > sparse_kq32_ibte.out

The reference result is:

====================================================================================================
Iteration number:   19
====================================================================================================
Conductivity(Siemens/m)           x                y                z
       x                3.4054e+07       4.1844e-10       3.7841e-11
       y                1.7484e-10       3.4054e+07      -1.5106e-11
       z                4.4490e-12      -2.9681e-11       3.4054e+07

Converged in 19 cycles with error = 5.2080e-06

In this tutorial, the IBTE result (\(3.4041\times 10^{7}\)) is larger than that of ERTA (\(2.7448\times 10^{7}\)), and is closer to the experimental value of \(3.659\times 10^{7}\) Siemens/m [10].

3. IBTE for QTrans + ABACUS

The ABACUS example is in tutorials/Al/abacus/conductivity/. It reads ABACUS data from ../data/ and uses nao_max: 40 and bands 5–7. Unlike the supplied OpenMX inputs, it already selects mob_level: ibte. The complete input-sparse.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 40
  Ham_type: abacus
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Al-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [32,32,32]
  q_size: [32,32,32]
  bands_indices: '5-7'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 40
  smearq: 40
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 120

conductivity:
  mob_level: ibte
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250

From the tutorial repository root, run:

cd tutorials/Al/abacus/conductivity/
mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config input-sparse.yaml > sparse_kq32_ibte.out

The reference IBTE result has equal diagonal conductivity components of \(5.2670 \times 10^7\) S/m and converges in 20 iterations, with a reported error of \(7.3239 \times 10^{-6}\) S/m. The reference ERTA result is \(4.1158 \times 10^7\) S/m. These are results for the supplied ABACUS data and settings; comparison with OpenMX requires consistent convergence tests.

Bulk bcc Fe

For ferromagnetic Fe, treat the two collinear spin channels separately.

The bulk bcc iron tutorial is located in tutorials/Fe/openmx/conductivity/. All necessary data files are available in tutorials/Fe/openmx/data/. Reference outputs are provided in tutorials/Fe/openmx/conductivity/ref/ , which can be used to compare with your own results to verify that QTrans is running correctly.

Enter into the directory, and there would be two yaml files: input-dense.yaml and input-sparse.yaml and the ref/ folder.

cd tutorials/Fe/openmx/conductivity/ && ls
input-dense.yaml  input-sparse.yaml ref/

1. ERTA for conductivity of ferromagnetic iron

In this tutorial, we set mob_level: erta to calculate spin-polarized conductivity on a coarse 16x16x16 k-point and q-point grids using ERTA.

By checking the input files input-dense.yaml or input-sparse.yaml, you will notice that we have added tags related to magnetism, such as magnetic_type: 'collinear' and magnetic_tolerance: 0.4. Place these tags in the advanced block. magnetic_type: collinear enables separate spin channels. The sparse input also sets magnetic_tolerance: 0.4 for magnetic symmetry detection.

Here we include the sixth to tenth bands by specifying bands_indices: '6-10', and adopt the default energy window defined by a half-width of 0.2 eV using over_band_edge: 0.2. This window is highlighted as the yellow region in Figure 3. The temperature is set to the room temperature with temperature: 300.0.

The complete input-dense.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  magnetic_type: 'collinear'

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[5.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 5, 0], [0, 0, 5]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Fe-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [16,16,16]
  q_size: [16,16,16]
  bands_indices: '6-10'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 25
  smearq: 25
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 75

conductivity:
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250
  mob_level: erta

Launch the QTrans calculation with:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-dense.yaml > dense_kq16_erta.out

At the end of the run, you should see output like this:

Conductivity[spin-1](Siemens/m)      x                y                z
            x              1.2325e+07        1.3380e-10        1.4600e-10
            y             -5.1509e-11        1.2325e+07        2.4725e-10
            z              1.7946e-10       -1.5949e-10        1.2325e+07
Conductivity[spin-2](Siemens/m)      x                y                z
            x              5.6797e+06        1.2500e-11        2.2015e-11
            y             -4.9999e-12        5.6797e+06        3.5765e-11
            z              3.7421e-11        3.7837e-11        5.6797e+06

Because of the ferromagnetism, there are two different spin channels of conductivity tensors: spin-1 is the majority spin channel, and spin-2 the minority one. The calculated conductivity of the majority spin is about twice that of the minority spin, which is attributed to the spin-dependent electronic band structures and spin-dependent scattering.

The complete input-sparse.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 14
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True
  magnetic_type: 'collinear'

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[5.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 5, 0], [0, 0, 5]]
  unitcell_filename: ../data/Fe-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../data/FORCE_SETS

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 0.5

transport:
  k_size: [16,16,16]
  q_size: [16,16,16]
  bands_indices: '6-10'
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 25
  smearq: 25
  gauss_type: -99
  e_thr: 75

conductivity:
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ibte_error: 0.00001
  ibte_cycle: 250
  mob_level: erta

The total conductivity is the sum of the two spin-channel tensors.

Perform the same calculation using the sparse gradient matrix:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-sparse.yaml > sparse_kq16_erta.out

The reference results are:

Conductivity[spin-1](Siemens/m)      x                y                z
            x              1.2330e+07       -1.2111e-10        8.4835e-11
            y              4.3807e-11        1.2330e+07       -3.7078e-10
            z              8.8611e-11       -7.7505e-11        1.2330e+07
Conductivity[spin-2](Siemens/m)      x                y                z
            x              5.6874e+06        4.3488e-11       -2.9390e-11
            y              2.3697e-11        5.6874e+06        1.0818e-11
            z             -2.0312e-12        1.1302e-11        5.6874e+06

Polar semiconductor GaAs

In this tutorial, we show how to compute the intrinsic electron mobility of the polar semiconductor GaAs using ERTA.

Polar materials exhibit long-range electron-phonon (e-ph) interactions between electrons and longitudinal optical (LO) phonons. These interactions pose challenges in achieving convergence in phonon-limited transport calculations. To address this, QTrans separates the electron-phonon coupling into two parts using the method described in ref [11] .

Here, we compute the long-range (polar) and short-range (nonpolar) contributions separately, using q-point importance sampling based on the Cauchy distribution. In the final step, the total mobility is obtained by combining the calculated scattering rates from both polar and nonpolar parts.

The GaAs tutorial is located in tutorials/GaAs/openmx/mobility/. All necessary data files are available in tutorials/GaAs/openmx/data/. The directory contains three calculations, which should be run in order:

cd tutorials/GaAs/openmx/mobility/ && ls
polar/ rmp/ total/

1. The long-range (polar) part

We first compute the long-range (polar) contribution by setting polar_split:'polar' in the conductivity block. In the input file input-polar.yaml, compared to nonpolar materials, additional parameters are required: the Born effective charges (BECs) and the dielectric constant (DL), which are necessary for applying the long-range correction (LRC). To activate LRC, the flag apply_correction: True must also be set.

The calculation of scattering rates in polar materials is memory demanding and typically requires ultra dense k/q-grid for convergence. To ensure the effective convergence of the integration results on the q-grid, QTrans employs Monte Carlo integration (MC_sampling) with importance sampling. Two sampling types are supported: 'uniform' and 'Cauchy'. In this tutorial, we use MC_sampling: 'Cauchy' and set the number of q-points to nsamples: 10000 to reduce computational time. The k-grid is set to 40x40x40. Here we use the sparse gradient matrix to speedup the calculations (read_sparse_grad_mat: True).

Note

One can increase the number of random q-points until the electron-phonon scattering rate is fully converged to obtain meaningful results.

We choose to use the default carrier concentration of \(1.0\times 10^{16}\) \(\text{cm}^{-3}\) for electrons by setting ncarrier: 10000000000000000. QTrans will automatically determine the Fermi level corresponding to the specified carrier concentration.

Note

Ensure that the concentration-dependent Fermi level lies within the specified energy window. Otherwise, QTrans may yield incorrect carrier concentrations and unreliable results.

The band structures of GaAs are shown in Figure 4. Here, we consider only the fifteenth band by specifying bands_indices: [15], since it is evident from the default energy window (over_band_edge: 0.2), as shown in Figure 5, that only the fifteenth band contributes within this range. This simplification is therefore reasonable and also helps reduce computational time and resource usage.

Enter polar/, where you will find the input file input-polar.yaml and the ref/ folder containing reference outputs:

cd polar/ && ls
input-polar.yaml ref/

The complete input-polar.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 19
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../../data/GaAs-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../../data/FORCE_SETS
  apply_correction: True
  BECs: [[[2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, 2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, 2.10569]],[[-2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, -2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, -2.10569]]]
  DL: [[13.355780, 0.000000, 0.000000],[0.000000, 13.355780, 0.000000],[0.000000, 0.000000, 13.355780]]

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 2.0

transport:
  k_size: [40,40,40]
  q_size: [40,40,40]
  bands_indices: [15]
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 10
  smearq: 10
  gauss_type: 0
  e_thr: 30

conductivity:
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ncarrier: 10000000000000000
  MC_sampling: 'Cauchy'
  polar_split: 'polar'
  nsamples: 10000

Now we are ready to launch the QTrans calculation with:

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-polar.yaml > k40q10000_polar.out

At the end of the run, you should see output like this:

Mobility(cm^2/V/s)           x                y                z
       x                2.8416e+02      -1.5685e-14       1.0457e-14
       y               -1.0457e-14       2.8416e+02      -1.0457e-14
       z               -2.0914e-14       0.0000e+00       2.8416e+02

cal_mode: 'conductivity' calculation will also output a file named rate_nk_polar.dat, which has the following format:

#Fermi level = -0.15378031 Hartree    Density of carrier = 4.51698351e-07
#ik_ibz  ibnd  weight_k          enk(Hartree)      scattering_rate(Hartree)
0        0     0.000031250000    -0.149761452883   3.4883742852896680e-05
1        0     0.000250000000    -0.143094385019   6.5879314145324497e-05

The second line defines the columns in the table: the irreducible Brillouin zone (IBZ) k-point index, the band index (relative to the band range bands_indices specified by the user in the input file), the weight of the k-point, the eigenvalue (energy), and the scattering rate. The indices and weights are dimensionless; the eigenvalues and scattering-rate energies are in Hartree. The remaining lines list the electronic states with non-zero scattering rates, along with their corresponding indices and values. This file will be used later for the calculation of total mobility.

2. The short-range (nonpolar) part

For the nonpolar part, we use the same set of tags as in the polar case, except setting variable polar_split to 'rmp' for calculation.

Enter rmp/, there would be a yaml file input-rmp.yaml and the ref/ folder containing reference outputs:

cd ..
cd rmp/ && ls
input-rmp.yaml ref/

Launch the QTrans calculation with:

The complete input-rmp.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 19
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../../data/GaAs-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../../data/FORCE_SETS
  apply_correction: True
  BECs: [[[2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, 2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, 2.10569]],[[-2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, -2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, -2.10569]]]
  DL: [[13.355780, 0.000000, 0.000000],[0.000000, 13.355780, 0.000000],[0.000000, 0.000000, 13.355780]]

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [2,2,2]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 2.0

transport:
  k_size: [40,40,40]
  q_size: [40,40,40]
  bands_indices: [15]
  temperature: 300.0
  smeark: 10
  smearq: 10
  gauss_type: 0
  e_thr: 30

conductivity:
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ncarrier: 10000000000000000
  MC_sampling: 'Cauchy'
  polar_split: 'rmp'
  nsamples: 10000

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-rmp.yaml > k40q10000_rmp.out

At the end of the run, you should see output like this:

Mobility(cm^2/V/s)           x                y                z
       x                1.9042e+03       4.1827e-14      -8.3654e-14
       y                4.1827e-14       1.9042e+03      -8.3654e-14
       z                0.0000e+00       0.0000e+00       1.9042e+03

There is also a scattering rate file named rate_nk_rmp.dat, which has the same structure as the file rate_nk_polar.dat.

3. Total mobility

Using the calculated scattering rates from the polar part (rate_nk_polar.dat) and nonpolar part (rate_nk_rmp.dat), we combine the state-resolved scattering rates to obtain the total mobility. Do not add the two scalar mobilities. Use rate files generated with matching k meshes, band selection, temperature, carrier concentration, and energy window.

At this stage, there is no need to recompute any scattering rates. Instead, we read them directly from the files by setting polar_rate_path: '../polar/rate_nk_polar.dat' and rmp_rate_path: '../rmp/rate_nk_rmp.dat' in the conductivity block.

Enter total/, there would be a yaml file named input-tot.yaml and the ref/ folder containing reference outputs:

cd ..
cd total/ && ls
input-tot.yaml ref/

Launch the QTrans calculation with:

The complete input-tot.yaml is:

basic:
  cal_mode: 'conductivity'
  graph_data_path_uc: ../../data/graph_data.npz
  nao_max: 19
  Ham_type: openmx
  outdir: './'

advanced:
  read_sparse_grad_mat: True

phonon:
  supercell_matrix: [[3.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0, 3, 0], [0, 0, 3]]
  unitcell_filename: ../../data/GaAs-pri.vasp
  force_infos_filename: ../../data/FORCE_SETS
  apply_correction: True
  BECs: [[[2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, 2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, 2.10569]],[[-2.10569, 0.00000, 0.00000],[0.00000, -2.10569, 0.00000],[0.00000, 0.00000, -2.10569]]]
  DL: [[13.355780, 0.000000, 0.000000],[0.000000, 13.355780, 0.000000],[0.000000, 0.000000, 13.355780]]

epc:
  grad_mat_path: ../../data/grad_mat_sparse.npy
  mat_info_sc_path: ../../data/mat_info_sc.npy
  cell_range_cut: [3,3,3]
  phonon_frequency_cutoff: 2.0

transport:
  k_size: [40,40,40]
  q_size: [40,40,40]
  bands_indices: [15]
  smeark: 10
  smearq: 10
  gauss_type: 0
  e_thr: 30

conductivity:
  over_band_edge: 0.2
  ncarrier: 10000000000000000
  polar_rate_path: '../polar/rate_nk_polar.dat'
  rmp_rate_path: '../rmp/rate_nk_rmp.dat'

mpirun -np 8 QTrans_run --config ./input-tot.yaml > k40q10000_tot.out

At the end of the run, you should get the total mobility in the output like this:

Mobility(cm^2/V/s)           x                y                z
       x                2.4726e+02      -1.5685e-14       4.1827e-14
       y                1.5685e-14       2.4726e+02       0.0000e+00
       z               -4.1827e-14       0.0000e+00       2.4726e+02

Note

The GaAs calculations shown here use very coarse parameters to save time for quick testing, and these results are far from convergence!

Note

The intrinsic hole mobility can be calculated accordingly by setting is_hole: True.

Note

The mobility of polar materials can also be computed using standard k/q-grids without Monte Carlo sampling by ERTA or IBTE, which typically has a slow convergence with respect to number of q-points. However, IBTE does not support random sampling for q-points.
